newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian nations buying cheap yen to pay back loans.
newsitem.headline: Asian nations buying cheap yen to pay back loans.

text.p: Asian nations, taking advantage of the recent slide of the yen, have been selling dollars against the Japanese currency in an apparent bid to build up money to pay off yen loans, traders in Tokyo said on Friday.
The fall in the yen's value has lessened the debt burden of Asian nations in yen terms, which has encouraged them to snap up the yen while it is cheap to use for repayments.
"It is quite reasonable for them to try to get supplies of yen to draw on because the yen has fallen sharply from last year," said a senior trader at a major Japanese bank.

The dollar, continuing its comeback from last year's record lows against the yen, hit a 42-month high of 114.92 yen in Tokyo on Tuesday. This was a 44 percent retracement from its post-war global low of 79.75 yen set on April 19, 1995.
Last year, the yen's sharp rise against the dollar drew complaints from some Southeast Asian nations as it inflated the burden of their loans from the Japanese government.
A Foreign Ministry official said the repayments are made every month, rather than on an annual basis. As of March, Asian nations had around $60 billion worth of yen loans outstanding.
Those which also hold yen-denominated assets in their external reserves may also need to buy the yen to try to prevent it from falling further, senior traders said.

They said an Indonesian government-related institution had placed offers to sell dollars at 114.50 yen on Thursday and 114.20 yen on Friday. This helped check the dollar's rise. Malaysia was also rumoured to have dollar-selling interest.
Meanwhile, a Chinese bank has been keen to sell dollars at around 115.00 yen to protect its options positions, dealers said.
A dealer at a European bank in Tokyo said the volume of combined offers by Asian operators was substantial, possibly amounting to several billion dollars.

Talk of dollar sales by Asian operators raised speculation that Japanese monetary authorities had discreetly encouraged their Asian counterparts to sell dollars to slow the pace of its rise against the Japanese currency, traders said.
A currency manager at a major Japanese bank said: "There is speculation that Asian nations are selling dollars on behalf of Japan."
A dollar rise well above 115 yen would be excessive and not justified by prevailing economic fundamentals, he added.
If the Bank of Japan moved to sell dollars directly, there would be a great risk of the dollar falling further than necessary, dealers said.
A senior Finance Ministry official declined to comment on the talk in the markets.

Japanese Finance Minister Watari Kubo said earlier this week that Japan may need to seriously consider taking action if fluctuations in exchange rates become too sudden or fail to reflect economic fundamentals.
Japanese business leaders have also voiced concern about an excessive rise in the dollar, which increases the costs of materials and products that they import from overseas.
Asian countries began taking out yen loans from the late 1950s to fund their economic development but the burden of the repayments has grown as the yen strengthened from the mid-1980s.

As of the end of March, total outstanding yen loans stood at 8.7766 trillion yen ($76.9 billion), of which Asian nations accounted for 6.7894 trillion yen ($59.5 billion), according to Finance Ministry statistics. ($1=114 yen) -- Tatsuo Ito, Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-3432-1396
